name: Endowment Effect
description: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire the same thing — ownership itself inflates perceived value.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to free trials, 'try before you buy' flows, and customization features that create a sense of ownership before purchase.
myth_risk_note: While the disputing Plott & Zeiler (10.1257/0002828054201387) paper exists with only 680 citations versus 5056+ for Kahneman & Knetsch's canonical work, the backing evidence is consistently replicated and applies broadly to psychological ownership contexts. The effect is not a zombie fact but has genuine methodological complexity regarding measurement.
prevalence_note: One of the most cited behavioral-economics findings outside academia entirely; standard in any pricing or ownership-framing design discussion.

findings.description: People demand substantially more to give up an object they own (willingness to accept) than they would pay to acquire the same object (willingness to pay) — demonstrated via real-market trading experiments; the Coase theorem predicted about half of randomly-endowed goods would trade, but observed trading volume was consistently and significantly lower, persisting even with market experience.
findings.source_title: Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem

findings.description: When experimental procedures are modified to remove subject misconceptions about the valuation-elicitation mechanism (anonymity, incentive-compatible training), the willingness-to-pay/willingness-to-accept gap largely disappears — suggesting much of the originally observed 'endowment effect' may reflect procedural artifacts and subject confusion rather than a stable psychological effect.
findings.source_title: The Willingness to Pay–Willingness to Accept Gap, the "Endowment Effect," Subject Misconceptions, and Experimental Procedures for Eliciting Valuations

applications.title: Blinkist's 'Saved Library' during onboarding
applications.description: Blinkist lets users save book summaries to a personal 'Library' during onboarding, before they've paid or fully committed -- giving users a sense of ownership over a curated collection that motivates them to complete the onboarding sequence.
applications.ethical_note: This is a genuine value-first mechanism -- users get something real (an actual saved summary) before any payment commitment, unlike patterns that manufacture a feeling of ownership without giving anything real. No deception or inflated claim involved.

applications.title: HEY Email pre-filling a new email address before signup completion
applications.description: HEY pre-populates a custom email address for a new user during the signup flow, before the account is actually finalized -- giving the address an 'it's already mine' quality intended to increase perceived ownership and follow-through.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine early preview of something real (the actual address they'll get), not a fabricated sense of ownership -- no deception involved, a clean illustration of the principle.

applications.title: Headspace's onboarding personalization quiz, with a noted execution gap
applications.description: Headspace asks new users about their goals (e.g. managing anxiety, sleeping better, relaxing) during onboarding to shape a personalized offer -- intended to build a sense of ownership over a tailored experience, though the source notes the specific goal options presented didn't always match what a given user actually wanted, undermining the intended effect.
applications.ethical_note: The intent here is genuinely user-beneficial (real personalization, not fabricated), but the source's own critique that the options didn't match actual user goals is worth keeping visible -- graded mixed rather than a clean user_beneficial, since good intent doesn't guarantee the user actually experienced the intended value.

applications.title: Trello's one-click background customization during onboarding
applications.description: Trello lets new users pick a background image for their board with a single click during onboarding, turning a generic productivity board into something visually personalized -- a small investment of customization effort intended to build a sense of ownership.
applications.ethical_note: A cosmetic customization choice with no deceptive framing or manufactured urgency -- users genuinely do own the choice they made, however small. Clean, low-stakes illustration of the principle.
